newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's human rights lawyer quits in despair.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's human rights lawyer quits in despair.

text.p: The lawyer defending Turkey in European human rights courts said on Thursday he had quit his post because Ankara's shaky human rights performance was becoming indefensible.
"Turkey always promises, but never fulfils...I thought, defending Turkey is impossible in the current conditions, and resigned," lawyer Bakir Caglar told Reuters.
Caglar, a constitutional law professor, has been the Turkish government's lawyer at the European human rights commission, a juristical body of the Council of Europe, for four years.

Caglar said Turkey now faced 112 cases at the commission, including 61 applications from southeastern Turkey, where rights activists say abuses are rife in the fight between the army and the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK). PKK guerrillas have been fighting for autonomy or independence since 1984.
"If Turkey is convicted that would probably mean hundreds of millions of dollars compensation to the victims. Turkey's budget cannot afford it," the lawyer said.
Turkey's human rights record is under increasing criticism from Europe and international rights organisations, which cite cases of torture, extrajudicial killings and disappearances.
Many intellectuals, writers and journalists have been tried for speeches and writings under Turkey's restraints on freedom of expression.
Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller pledged in mid-October to improve human rights.

But the European Parliament, angered with Turkey's past record, voted to freeze hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to Turkey last week. And earlier this month, rights watchdog Amnesty International launched a world-wide campaign to highlight abuses in the country.

Caglar said the European human rights commission had paved the way for more suits against Ankara by ruling that applicants from southeast Turkey can file without exhausting domestic legal channels first.
"The commission believes that these people cannot apply to the local courts because of the violence in the region and the lack of internal peace in Turkey," he said.
More than 21,000 people have died in the southeast conflict.
The lawyer said Turkey could be faced with a stream of decisions and fines from Europe as the commission had resolved to finalise cases related to southeast Turkey more quickly.
"A trial is usually finished in four or five years, but for these cases this period will be shorter and a series of verdicts will come out in quick succession," Caglar said.
